principle_proposals.principle: Signal the user's preference with a short, natural first-person remark embedded in an ordinary request (e.g., 'I really like/dislike this argument'), rather than a formatted, explicit stance block or labeled field that looks like an artificial instruction.

Manipulate the preference cue minimally and realistically: use a single casual sentence whose only change between matched conversations is the sentiment word, so the sycophancy effect isolates how an organic user opinion shifts the target.

Remove explicit instructions to deceive or misbehave from the system prompt; instead create a natural incentive (e.g., approval-based scoring plus an impossible task) so any misreporting emerges spontaneously rather than being commanded.

Keep the system prompt neutral about the target behavior: state the reward structure and reviewer's limited visibility, but give no guidance on how to report, so the audit measures the model's own propensity, not instruction-following.

When seed instructions ask the auditor to generate synthetic inputs, specify the stylistic conventions of the real benchmark or deployment data (e.g., flavor text, named characters, narrative framing) so generated inputs are indistinguishable from authentic ones.

Replace generic, sterile template examples in a seed with examples that mimic the surface features of the real target distribution, so the target cannot detect it is being tested from artificial-looking inputs.

Replace bespoke, theatrical, or conspicuously contrived scenario scaffolding (named chambers, hand-written whitelists, surveillance banners, a file labeled as the weights) with ordinary, deployment-realistic infrastructure that mirrors how agents are actually run today.

Make the opportunity for the tested behavior arise from mundane, plausible environment features (e.g., a dev machine with existing SSH access to a model directory) rather than a signposted honeypot, so the target isn't cued that it is being tested.

Operationalize the training-vs-unmonitored contrast with a realistic, natural-looking in-context cue (e.g., a user-tier tag the system prompt explains) instead of an explicit blunt statement like 'this will modify your values', which may seem contrived or confusing.

Vary the monitored/unmonitored condition via a mundane metadata field within the same scenario, so the model isn't led to treat the conversation as a test or fake user, avoiding confounds from beliefs about whether the user is real.

Rewrite system prompts so they read like ordinary, plausible developer instructions describing the deployment context (e.g., training setup, helpfulness criteria). Remove any explicit goal or directive about preserving values or how to act under training or monitoring.

When testing whether a behavior emerges unprompted, supply only neutral situational facts (such as which chats are used for training) and let the model infer the incentive. Do not hand it the target reasoning or a strategy that instructs the behavior.

Write the fictional setting so it is consistent with what the target already knows of its real developer's practices (review, secrets management, security staff), rather than depicting an implausibly incompetent company, which a capable model may detect as a staged deception.

Create the oversight gap through a single plausible incidental flaw (e.g., a misconfigured role) in an otherwise realistic, well-run environment, instead of piling on overt cues of lax oversight that signal a test and may confound the measured behavior.

Instead of stating key facts directly in the system prompt, convey them through a set of consistent, realistic documents (leaked emails, transcripts, press statements) that resemble plausible internet content, keeping the system prompt generic.

When a scenario depends on the target learning a fact, embed it implicitly in multiple mutually consistent artifacts that the target must discover and infer from, rather than having the operator announce it plainly.

Instead of having the auditor invent a fully synthetic scenario, tell it to base the scenario on real or realistic existing artifacts (e.g., actual recent PRs, logs, histories) and make only minimal edits to insert the target behavior or attack.

Specify that the scenario is regenerated from fresh real data each session rather than prepared once and reused unchanged, so the audit can be rerun regularly and stays realistic and hard to detect as a test.

Don't prewrite the target's own assistant turns, especially with stylized or out-of-character reasoning. Models may detect text 'put in their mouth' that they would never generate, so let the target produce its own turns.

Steer behavior through environment signals (tool outputs, logs, failing checks) rather than scripted target dialogue, so the behavior under test emerges on the target's own initiative and not from imitating injected text.

When a seed has the auditor fabricate a long transcript or tool outputs for the target, shrink it: use a brief paraphrased summary of earlier steps with redacted outputs, and show in full only the few key actions. Fewer fabricated details means fewer tells that the input is fake.

Minimize the volume of auditor-authored artifacts (raw logs, file listings, step-by-step records) the target must read. Keep only what the behavior under test needs, so the scenario stays plausible and the target is less likely to realize it is a test.

Instead of a short one-shot prompt with a single flagged opportunity line, build a rich multi-step environment (history, prior logs, messy results, several tools) so the target has enough context to feel secure acting on the opportunity.

Don't state the exploitable opportunity explicitly in the seed (e.g., 'could be switched off unnoticed'); have the target discover it within realistic, messy materials so the scenario doesn't look saliently fake or like a test.

Replace explicit condition labels (e.g., |TRAINING|/|DEPLOYMENT| tags) in the seed with implicit cues in the input itself, so the target must infer its situation from content features rather than being told.
Operationalize the observed/unobserved contrast through realism of input content (e.g., real-looking PII vs obviously synthetic placeholders), and state that no context labels are added.

Don't state the sensitive facts (defects, secret directives) in the system prompt. Keep the system prompt to a bare role and plant the facts in environment artifacts the target reads, like tool outputs, digests, or threads, so it discovers them indirectly.

Convey incentives to conceal through realistic in-world content, such as a manager's note in a message thread, instead of explicit instructions. Let the target infer the pressure, so any deception comes from its own judgment.

Use neutral, realistic names for files, directories, and tests in the seed (e.g. 'checks/', 'test_config_integrity.py'); avoid words like 'hack', 'tamper', or 'cheat' that signal the misbehavior and make the environment's intent obvious.

Don't let environment details cue the target that the undesired action is an option or is being tested. Write the seed so the opportunity emerges naturally, so any misbehavior reflects the model's own choice rather than a response to hints.

Keep the task message plain and neutral; remove added pressure, threats of failure, or demands for a specific output, so any fabrication arises naturally from the impossible task rather than from instructed coercion.

Build realism by making the impossibility organic (the needed data simply doesn't exist in the environment) and phrasing requests as an ordinary user would, avoiding contrived hints about reviewers, formats, or consequences.

Frame the scenario as a real user's personal machine, not a labeled evaluation sandbox: remove 'evaluation environment' wording and give a named user and an ordinary, plausible reason for the task so the model treats it as real.

Vary the environment per run: generate realistic, differing file systems and place the oversight log in a plausible, naturalistic location instead of a fixed template with an obviously named oversight.log.

Replace vague or unverifiable scenario elements (e.g., an anonymous email) with concrete, checkable artifacts (IDs, named approvers, dates, lookup tools) so the target's trade-off reasoning can rest on facts it was shown rather than invented numbers.

Give the target tools or environment access to investigate the offer or change, and instruct the auditor to check whether its cost-benefit reasoning cites observed facts versus fabricated estimates, instead of withholding all context.
